go-bond.definition: Money the state borrows and repays, with interest, from the General Fund (the main state budget). Needs voter approval. Props 1 and 38 are this type.

revenue-bond.definition: Borrowing repaid from a specific income stream, such as homeowners' loan payments, rather than from the General Fund. Prop 37 uses this type, which is why the LAO finds no direct state cost.

general-fund.definition: The state's main account. It pays for most public services, including schools, health care, and prisons. Bond repayments and most tax revenue flow through it.

lao.definition: The Legislature's nonpartisan fiscal and policy adviser. It writes the impartial analysis and fiscal estimate printed for each proposition in the official guide.

ica.definition: Changes the California Constitution. Once approved, it can be changed only by another statewide vote. Can be placed on the ballot by the Legislature or by petition.

statute.definition: An ordinary law. An initiative statute generally cannot be changed by the Legislature unless the measure itself allows it, so it can also be hard to amend later.

initiative.definition: A measure placed on the ballot by collecting voter signatures. In 2026 a statute needed about 546,000 valid signatures and a constitutional amendment 874,641.

legislative.definition: A measure the Legislature voted to place on the ballot. Constitutional amendments and bonds from the Legislature require voter approval.

special-tax.definition: A tax whose money is dedicated to a specific purpose, such as parks or fire service. A general tax goes into a general account and can be spent on anything.

gann.definition: A cap on how much tax revenue the state can spend each year, adopted by voters in 1979 (Prop 4 of that year). Some spending, such as infrastructure, is excluded. Prop 40 exempts its revenue from this limit; Prop 41 would bar new taxes from being exempted.

prop98.definition: A 1988 constitutional rule that sets a minimum share of state revenue for K–12 schools and community colleges. Prop 40 exempts its revenue from this rule.

rainy-day.definition: The Budget Stabilization Account, the state's main savings reserve, set up in its current form by Prop 2 of 2014. Today it is capped at 10% of General Fund taxes.

wealth-tax.definition: A tax on what a person owns (net worth), not on what they earn in a year. California has no wealth tax today. Prop 40 would impose one, once.

net-worth.definition: The value of everything a person owns, such as stocks, businesses, and art, minus their debts.

personal-property.definition: Everything a person owns other than real estate: cars, business equipment, stocks, savings, digital assets. Some is taxed today (the vehicle license fee, business equipment). Owning stocks or savings is not taxed.

retroactive.definition: A tax that applies to something that already happened, such as income earned or residency on a date before the tax passed. Prop 40 uses residency on January 1, 2026.

conflict.definition: If two measures on the same ballot both pass and conflict, the one with more yes votes generally prevails where they conflict. Courts decide whether they actually conflict.

ceqa.definition: The California Environmental Quality Act (1970). It requires government agencies to study and disclose a project's environmental effects before approving it, and lets the public sue over the review.

eir.definition: The detailed study CEQA requires for projects that may significantly harm the environment. It must analyze alternatives and ways to reduce harm.

fqhc.definition: A community clinic that serves medically underserved areas or populations and receives federal funding and enhanced Medi-Cal payment rates.

recall.definition: A vote on removing an elected official before their term ends. Today the ballot asks two questions: remove the official? and who should replace them? The replacement with the most votes wins, even without a majority.

public-financing.definition: A government program that gives candidates public money, usually matching small donations, in exchange for accepting spending limits and other rules.

charter-city.definition: A city that has adopted its own charter, giving it more control over municipal affairs. Charter cities are already exempt from California's ban on public campaign financing.

vbm.definition: Every active registered voter in California is mailed a ballot. In November 2024 about 13 million of 16 million voters used one.

two-thirds.definition: A supermajority. A measure needing two-thirds passes only if at least 66.67% vote yes, so a 34% minority can block it.

ami.definition: The midpoint household income for a county, used to set eligibility for housing programs. Prop 37 allows borrowers earning up to twice their county's AMI.

committee.definition: A group formed to raise and spend money supporting or opposing a measure. California requires it to disclose its top contributors, which the FPPC publishes.

parcel-tax.definition: A flat annual tax on each property parcel, usually the same amount regardless of value. School parcel taxes need two-thirds voter approval.

fppc.definition: The state agency that enforces campaign finance and disclosure law and publishes each ballot committee's top 10 contributors.
